title: Week 3: Make it standalone

series.title: Physical AI Lab: Cardboard Robot (4 week course)

summary: Optional: bring your own Raspberry Pi and USB speakerphone, and the Pi becomes the robot's brain, with the speakerphone as its ears and voice and the Week 2 battery powering everything. Then unplug it and walk away with it. No Pi? Your robot stays on your laptop and you spend the session in Deepgram's voice studio.
detail: This week is optional and bring-your-own: if you want your robot to run without a laptop, bring a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 that you've set up at home, plus a USB speakerphone (the steps are under Before you start). The Pi runs Chromium and opens this same page, so your robot works exactly as before. You control the Pi from your laptop with Raspberry Pi Connect while you set it up, then close it and carry your robot away. No Pi? Your robot keeps running from your laptop, and you work through the voice studio track instead.
outcome: Pi track: a robot that talks, moves its mouth and turns its head with no laptop and no wall plug. No Pi: a sharper personality and a robot tuned for a noisy room.
artifact: A fully wireless talking cardboard robot, or a better-tuned laptop robot.
prereqs: Your robot from Week 2, with its power bank charged. Your laptop and your Deepgram key.

Doing the Pi upgrade? Bring a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 (2 GB or more) with its memory card and power supply, set up at home as below, and a USB speakerphone (any brand, for example an EMEET M0 Plus). No Pi? Skip the rest of this list.
Power, pick one. Free: the 10,000 mAh power bank you got in Week 2. It runs a Pi robot for about 3 hours. Upgrade: buy your own bigger battery and bring it in. It runs about twice as long.

Optional upgrade list, to match the instructor's robot. Buy these yourself: ☐ Raspberry Pi 5 (4 GB) ☐ Raspberry Pi 5 Active Cooler ☐ 32 GB microSD card ☐ Official Raspberry Pi 27 W USB-C power supply, for setting up at home ☐ USB speakerphone, for example an EMEET M0 Plus ☐ Anker 20,000 mAh power bank with a USB-C port rated 30 W or more. Already have a Pi 4? Keep it and just add the power bank.

1. On your computer, install Raspberry Pi Imager from raspberrypi.com/software and use it to put Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit, with desktop) on the memory card. In its settings, add a username and password and the Hub's wifi from your event email.
2. Start the Pi once with a screen, keyboard and mouse, and finish the welcome steps.
3. Turn on Raspberry Pi Connect (its icon is in the top bar) and sign in with a free Raspberry Pi ID. On your laptop, check you can see the Pi's screen at connect.raspberrypi.com.
4. Plug in your speakerphone, check the Pi plays sound through it, then open Chromium and visit this page once, so it's ready.

slides.title: Week 3: Make it standalone
bullets: Brought a Raspberry Pi? Tonight it takes over from your laptop, running on the battery you already have.
No Pi? Your robot stays on your laptop, and you take the voice studio track.
Either way, Deepgram does the listening and talking.
slides.note: Ask for a show of hands: who brought a Pi? Seat Pi people together so helpers can work the tables.

slides.title: What each robot needs this week
bullets: ☐ Your robot from Week 2, with its Pico and breadboard
☐ A charged power bank: the free one from Week 2, or your own upgrade
Pi track: ☐ your Raspberry Pi 4 or 5, set up at home, and its power supply
Pi track: ☐ your USB speakerphone
Pi track: ☐ 1 × USB-A to micro-USB data cable, for the Pico (on the table)
Pi track: ☐ 1 × short cable from the power bank to the Pi's USB-C port (on the table)
Pi track: ☐ Velcro strips or tape
Bring: your laptop and your Deepgram key
slides.note: Attendees bring the Pi, its memory card and a USB speakerphone; we supply the cables. Helper table: a setup station with a screen, keyboard, mouse and micro-HDMI cable for anyone whose Pi isn't set up yet; spare cables; spare charged power banks. A Pi 5 run from a power bank limits its USB ports, so it may warn about power; that's fine for this build because the servos run from the breadboard.

slides.title: Two ways to power it
bullets: Free: the 10,000 mAh power bank from Week 2. About 3 hours on a Pi.
Upgrade: your own 20,000 mAh power bank with a 30 W USB-C port, like the instructor's robot. About twice as long.
Either way: the Pi goes in the USB-C port and the servo lead goes in the other port.
The upgrade list is on this page, under Before you start.
slides.note: Nobody has to buy anything: the free power bank works. Helper table: spare charged free power banks for anyone who forgot theirs.

slides.title: Plug in the Pi
bullets: Speakerphone into a blue USB port on the Pi.
Unplug the Pico from your laptop and plug it into another blue port, with the USB-A cable.
Power the Pi from the power bank's other port.
Put the Pi and battery on the floor of the base box, under the neck, and fix them with velcro or tape. Cut a small notch at the back for the charging cable.
slides.note: Done when: the Pi's light flickers and the speakerphone lights up. The battery is the heaviest part, so on the floor of the base keeps the robot from tipping. Tip: tape the base floor on one side only, like a hinge, so you can open it to charge or fix things.

slides.title: Open the Pi from your laptop
bullets: On your laptop, go to connect.raspberrypi.com and open your Pi's screen.
On the Pi, open Chromium and go to this lesson page.
slides.note: If someone's Pi didn't come up on the wifi, send them to the setup station.

slides.title: Set it up on the Pi
bullets: Paste your Deepgram key and connect the robot, like Week 1.
Pick the speakerphone if Chromium asks for a microphone.
Set the mouth and neck sliders again. They're saved on the Pi.
Start talking.
slides.note: The speakerphone sits right next to the robot, so keep Speaker is inside the box switched on.

slides.title: Make it a better talker
bullets: Write a second personality and see which one guests will like better.
Make it a quiz host: it asks questions and keeps score in its head.
Tune Patience for a noisy room. Does it still know when you're done?
Write a greeting that changes with the weather: ask it to check first.
slides.note: Everything here runs on the laptop, exactly like Weeks 1 and 2. Pair a no-Pi person with a Pi person for the walk test at the end.

slides.title: Walk away with it
bullets: Pi track: close the Pi on your laptop, check nothing is plugged into a wall or laptop, then pick the robot up and carry it to another table. Keep talking.
No Pi? Show your new personality to a Pi builder, and hear theirs.
slides.note: Done when: it holds a conversation on the far side of the room.

slides.title: Week 4: Demo day
bullets: Teach it a new trick and polish it.
Then show it off to guests.
Bring it fully charged. Laptop robots are welcome on stage too.

flow.title: Pi track: move it onto the Pi
Run your robot
flow.note: Pi track: open this page in Chromium on the Raspberry Pi. No Pi: use it on your laptop as usual.

troubleshooting: The Pi isn't on the wifi, or Connect can't find it: take it to the setup station and fix the wifi with a screen and keyboard.
Connect robot does nothing on the Pi: open the page in Chromium, not another browser.
Connect robot shows nothing on the Pi: the Pico cable is charge-only. Swap it for a data cable.
The robot can't hear you: in Chromium, click the lock icon and pick your speakerphone as the microphone.
No sound: set your speakerphone as the Pi's audio output in the speaker menu at the top right.
The Pi shows a lightning bolt or restarts: the battery port can't keep up. Try the other port or a thicker cable, or plug in your Pi's own power supply for now.
The battery switches itself off: some power banks sleep on low current. Press its button to wake it.
